candidates.title: Cliques dissolve against a shared opponent
candidates.detail: The episode's mechanism is textbook intergroup psychology. Muzafer Sherif's 1954 Robbers Cave study divided 22 boys into two groups, manufactured hostility between them, then found that contact and conversation did not fix it - only 'superordinate goals', tasks too big for one group alone, did. By the end roughly two thirds of the boys' friendship choices crossed group lines. The episode stages both halves: a common antagonist, and then a shared task. NOTE: nobody connected with the show has cited Sherif; this is a mapping, not a claimed influence, and the card must say so.
candidates.moment: Three position-based cliques stop being three the moment a rival quiz team turns on one of them.

candidates.title: Sharon Fieldstone wrote a book, and its title is an argument
candidates.detail: Dr Sharon Fieldstone (Sarah Niles) returns, now a professor of sports psychology, promoting a book reported as 'Unlocking the I in Team'. The title inverts the oldest cliche in team sport - there is no I in team - and the episode then proves the book's point: the squad does not cohere until the individuals inside it become legible to one another. REVIEWER: the exact book title comes from a search summary of recap coverage; corroborate it before it ships, and drop the title if only one source has it.

candidates.title: Trent Crimm is a podcaster now, and he is narrating
candidates.detail: James Lance returns as Trent Crimm, who has left the paper and the book behind and now hosts a podcast (reported as 'Through the Laces'). His interview with Sharon is used as the episode's framing device - the two of them describe the problem in the abstract while the episode shows it happening. The show has used Trent as an outside observer since season one; this is the first time it lets him narrate.

candidates.title: Ted has never read Harry Potter
candidates.detail: Alice tries to explain the three cliques using Harry Potter's central trio and it lands on nobody, because Ted has never read the books - reportedly because Henry went for Percy Jackson instead. Beard translates via Ferris Bueller. The joke is also the episode's thesis in miniature: the coaches cannot describe the team's problem because the room has no shared frame of reference.

candidates.title: The cliques are drawn along position lines
candidates.detail: The squad has split into attackers, midfielders and defenders - not by age, nationality or status, but by job. Recaps describe the split in character terms (logical midfielders, anxious defenders, selfish attackers) and it boils over in the changing room over small things: socks, and a refusal to swap shirt numbers. Football itself made the factions; the tactical structure of the sport is the thing dividing them.

candidates.title: What finally unites them is being underestimated together
candidates.detail: The thing that ends the factions is not a drill or a speech. A rival quiz team abuses the players and pours a drink over one of them, and the squad answers as one. Multiple reviews land on the same reading: their common ground is the experience of being dismissed, and the episode is honest that this is a grim way to find each other. It also rhymes with the season's stated subject - a women's team nobody outside the building takes seriously.

candidates.title: The punishment is to go back and clean it up
candidates.detail: Ted's discipline for the brawl is reported as making the squad run to the pub and clean it. That is restitution rather than penalty - the wrong is repaired where it happened, in front of the person who was wronged, rather than paid off in laps. It is also the most consistent thing the character does: the response to a mess is to go back to it.

candidates.title: Tracey Ullman was the only name they considered
candidates.detail: Zelda Southport, managing partner of a firm investing solely in women's sport, is played by Tracey Ullman. Brendan Hunt has said the part was first imagined as a younger male executive; once they made her older than Rebecca, so she could be a mentor - something Rebecca has rarely had, and never from a woman - Ullman was the first and only name raised. Hunt describes the cast as giddy when she signed.

candidates.title: Ted has run this play before
candidates.detail: At least one review reads the episode as a deliberate rhyme with season one's 'Two Aces', where Ted's answer to a divided squad was also a staged, faintly ridiculous group ritual - the midnight curse-lifting ceremony - that worked for reasons other than the ones advertised. REVIEWER: one outlet makes the comparison explicitly; treat the parallel as an interpretation rather than a production fact, and check whether the S1 episode number given anywhere is right (Two Aces is S1E6).
